utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, there are just a few preliminary matters I would ask to address the Chamber in private session, if I may.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I have one announcement to make about hearing times, and we hope this won't cause inconvenience. It's become necessary to rearrange dates in early June. We will sit, there will be a hearing day on the 2nd, Monday the 2nd of June, but not Friday the 6th. As I say, I hope that doesn't cause inconvenience.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: It doesn't, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It doesn't. I'm glad to hear that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Let the witness take the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you'd like to take a seat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm not sure if the Chamber would want, but I would offer to the Chamber, if the Chamber wants, for me to make any inquiries from the witness about the matters we've just discussed regarding the waiver.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It may be more straightforward at the moment to deal with the rest of the evidence and then you can reconsider that position.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, I'd ask we begin your testimony by having you see tab 1 of a new exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'd ask if we could assign a number to this package of 14 exhibits.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, Prosecutor's Exhibit 450.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, I'd ask you to take a look at Prosecution Exhibit 450, tab 1, and my question to you, I'd ask you to take a look at the B/C/S version and ask you, is that your name on the top line of that exhibit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-161
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And does that document accurately reflect your work and professional experience?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-161
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm finished with that exhibit. Thank you. I'd ask that that document be tendered under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, I'm going to ask you to help orient the Chamber to some of the people you will testify regarding. I'm going to ask you if you know certain people, and I will ask you to tell us in a sentence or two who these people are. The first person I would ask you to describe for us is a person by the name of Petar Mihajlovic. Do you know who he is? And if so, tell us who he is.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-161
utterances.text: Yes, I do know Mr. Petar Mihajlovic. He was an employee of the Federal Secretariat for Internal Affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: How about a person by the name of Zdravko Ljubinkovic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-161
utterances.text: Yes, I know Mr. Zdravko Ljubinkovic as well. He's a businessman in Ljubljana.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: A person by the name of Predrag Jesuric.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-161
utterances.text: Yes, I do know Mr. Predrag Jesuric. He was head of the SUP in Bijeljina. I think he's still working there in the SUP of Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: The person by the name of Branko Popovic, also known as Marko Pavlovic.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-161
utterances.text: Yes, I met Mr. Marko Pavlovic as well at the beginning of the war in Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And what position, if any, did he have in Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-161
utterances.text: At the time, he held the position of the commander of the Territorial Defence of the municipality of Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: By what name was he known in Zvornik during the spring of 1992?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-161
utterances.text: He was known under the name of Marko Pavlovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did there come a time after that when you learnt that his real name was Brano Popovic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-161
utterances.text: Yes. I learnt that his name was Branko Popovic and that he lives in Sombor.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now I'll ask you about a person by the name of Aleksandar Sekanic.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-161
utterances.text: Yes. He was Marko Pavlovic's assistant. He comes from the village of Bilosevac in Bijeljina municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: The next person I'd ask you about is Ratko Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-161
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Ratko Vidovic is chief of the Department for Internal Affairs in Mali Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: A person by the name of Dragan Spasojevic.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-161
utterances.text: Dragan Spasojevic was the chief of the traffic department in Veliki Zvornik, municipality of Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Fadil Mujic.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-161
utterances.text: Fadil Mujic was the chief of the crime service in the SUP of Zvornik municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: A person by the name of Rade Kostic.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-161
utterances.text: Rade Kostic was a police commander in Beli Manastir.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did you ever see the car that Rade Kostic would drive in?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-161
utterances.text: Yes. It was a jeep with "M" plates, meaning the Ministry of Internal Affairs of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can I ask you to describe what do you know about the relationship between Rade Kostic and Marko Pavlovic.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-161
utterances.text: Their relationship was such that they had a private conflict, and Marko Pavlovic told me that Rade Kostic was looting in the territory of Baranja, and he once brought an anonymous letter allegedly written by citizens from the area. And Rade Kostic said that he had information that Marko Pavlovic was looting in the territory of Eastern Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I want to ask you now about a person -- I want to ask you now about a person by the name of Stevo Radic.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-161
utterances.text: Stevo Radic was in the local authorities of Zvornik municipality, in the municipal authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And now about a person by the name of Marko Pejic.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-161
utterances.text: Marko Pejic was the deputy to the commander of paramilitary units known as the Tigers.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, during the course of your travels in Serbia, did you ever have occasion to see vehicles belonging to Arkan's Tigers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-161
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: How is it that you were able to identify them as belonging to that particular organisation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-161
utterances.text: Because they had the emblem of a Tiger on them.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Are you familiar with where the headquarters of this organisation was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-161
utterances.text: Yes. It was in Ljutica Bogdan Street, next to the Red Star stadium, in the house of Zeljko Raznjatovic, Arkan.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did you ever have occasion to see armed personnel outside that house?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-161
utterances.text: Yes, I did. There were armed men guarding the house there.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I want to now draw your attention to a person by the name -- I'm sorry, before I leave Mr. Pejic; was he also known by another name?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-161
utterances.text: His nickname was Peja.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'd like to now draw your attention to a person by the name of Vojin Vukovic. Are you familiar with that person?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-161
utterances.text: Yes. I heard him -- I saw him in passing maybe two times. He had his own group of armed men.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Do you know the name of that group?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-161
utterances.text: Yellow Wasps, and they were in Zvornik. Their name was Yellow Wasps.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, Vojin Vukovic, was he also known by an alias or another name?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-161
utterances.text: His nickname was Zuca, The Yellow One.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, I want to draw your attention to some well known members of the Serbian MUP, and I would ask you, can you describe for the Chamber who was Obrad Stevanovic.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-161
utterances.text: Obrad Stevanovic was the head of the police department in the Secretariat of Internal Affairs, and later he became assistant minister.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Radmilo Bogdanovic.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-161
utterances.text: Radmilo Bogdanovic was the Minister of Internal Affairs in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Who became the Minister of Internal Affairs after Radmilo Bogdanovic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-161
utterances.text: After Radmilo Bogdanovic, Mr. Zoran Sokolovic became Minister of Internal Affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And finally with respect to the Serbian MUP, I would ask you about a person by the name of Mile Puzovic.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-161
utterances.text: Mile Puzovic was the head of the Department for Frontier Affairs and Foreigners, aliens.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: The last name that I would ask you to describe whether you know this person is a person by the name of Tomica Raicevic.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-161
utterances.text: Tomica Raicevic was an official in the government of the Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'd like to now draw your attention to the relationship between the federal MUP and the Bosnian Serb MUP. Were you aware of a relationship between these two organisations?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I draw the Chamber's attention to paragraph 43.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I was familiar with that relationship.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Is that something you can describe for the Chamber at this point in time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-161
utterances.text: The relationship was such that the federal MUP had the -- adopted the position that it should assist the leadership in Republika Srpska. They had a coordinator, and they frequently held meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I want to now ask you some questions or draw your attention to Eastern Bosnia. During the spring and summer of 1992, did you have occasion to travel frequently in the area of Eastern Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-161
utterances.text: Yes. I travelled very frequently; every three or four days.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can you describe the municipalities which you frequented during that period of time.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-161
utterances.text: In Serbia, I frequented Ruma, Sremska Mitrovica, Sabac, Loznica, Mali Zvornik, Ljubovija, Bajina Basta, Uzice. And in the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Bijeljina and Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I want to draw your attention to Bijeljina. During the course of your travels there, did you come to learn about Arkan's presence in that municipality?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-161
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can you tell us the basis of how you learnt that information.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-161
utterances.text: I came to see [redacted]who have houses at the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. entrance to Bijeljina in -- coming from the direction of Bogatic municipality. When I arrived, I was told that the war had started in Bijeljina the previous night. I couldn't reach the centre of town. I stayed with my brothers that evening. I heard reports that there were some troops close to Bijeljina. When I went towards Serbia, I was told that they were located on the road between the village of Popovi and the crossing at Drina across which there was a raft, like a small ferry. And not far from the road I noticed some men there, and I came across the army, and I asked them, "Whose army are you?" And they said, "Can't you see that we are the Serbian army?" In front of the army a gentleman came who introduced himself as a major by the name of Marko Pejic. I stayed there for a while and then I went on to Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, I would just remind you, in an effort to protect your identity, it may not be necessary to mention the specific relationship that you have, specific familiar relationship to some of these non-essential people. I will be asking the Chamber to redact that reference but remind you that, unless it's necessary, please don't express these familial relationships.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I would also ask at this time that Prosecution tab 2 be placed in front of the witness. This is an exhibit that I anticipate I will use during different times of his testimony. I would ask that it be left on the desk in front of him.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, I want to ask you a few specific questions about your observations in Bijeljina. The place where you met this Peja, can you describe, was there any accommodation set up in that area?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-161
utterances.text: Yes. There were quite a number of men there. There were tents. There was a generator to produce electricity, and I saw two wounded men sitting there. And he said that they were brave fighters who were suffering and waiting patiently for a helicopter to transfer them to the hospital in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, the tents that you saw there, based on your experience, what capacity or how many people could be accommodated in the tents that you observed at that location?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-161
utterances.text: About a hundred men.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And to be clear, the location where you made these observations, what republic was that in?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-161
utterances.text: In the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Between the Drina River and the first settlement, called Popovi.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did it appear to you that the tents and the generator and the other things that you saw there had been set up very recently or had been there for some period of time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-161
utterances.text: It was night-time, and I really couldn't say. They were dug in a little bit because the ground was not level, so certainly a couple of days prior to this.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Was there something about the car that you were driving on this night that you believe allowed you to drive in and out of that location?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-161
utterances.text: Yes. I had official registration plates, and that certainly helped, because if I had had civilian registration plates, there would have been problems for me.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: You've testified about seeing some wounded men there. Was any statement made to you about what was going to happen or what was being done for those wounded men?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-161
utterances.text: Yes. I saw two wounded men, and their commander said that they were brave, that they were suffering quietly and that they were waiting to be transported by helicopter to Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Prior to you leaving this scene, did any helicopter arrive at this location?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-161
utterances.text: No, it didn't. It was night-time, about 2200 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did there come a time later that you saw a picture of this Peja who you've described in a helicopter?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-161
utterances.text: Yes, I did, with a singer of light music. He was also wearing a uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: The helicopter depicted in this photograph that you saw, was it a private helicopter?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-161
utterances.text: It was a military helicopter, a Gazelle.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: During this time period, how many times did you go into the centre of Bijeljina?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-161
utterances.text: I was in the centre of Bijeljina twice during that initial period.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'd ask that we talk about each one separately. Can you describe for the Chamber your best recollection about your first visit. When was the first visit you made to Bijeljina during this time period?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-161
utterances.text: The first time I went was about three or four days later - I don't know exactly - and I reached the centre. There were troops lined up which were being reviewed by Mr. Zeljko Raznjatovic. I heard that in the youth centre some people had come from the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Fikret Abdic and Mrs. Biljana Plavsic, and that they were talking there at the time. I stayed for a while. I didn't see them. I didn't see Mr. Abdic or Biljana Plavsic. That was my first visit.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I want to ask you a specific question about the people -- about the soldiers that you say you saw lined up. Approximately how many, and did they appear to be all under the command of Arkan?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-161
utterances.text: There were about 200 soldiers, and they were all under his command. They were well equipped, well dressed, wearing modern uniforms. He too was in uniform. And he reviewed them, and they were preparing some kind of a military review.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: This review that you are describing, was it more in the nature of a simple roll call or was it more in the nature of some type of ceremonial presentation of these troops?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-161
utterances.text: Yes. It was a ceremonial presentation for somebody who was due to come and inspect the troops.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: While you were present in Bijeljina this time, was there a particular story with respect to Arkan that was being spoken about very widely among the people of Bijeljina?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-161
utterances.text: Yes. Everyone was talking about Arkan as a great soldier, how capable his unit was. They spoke in the village that they were unbelievably well trained and equipment.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Was there a discussion about an event at that occurred between Arkan and a commander of the garrison, the JNA garrison, in Bijeljina?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-161
utterances.text: Yes. The story was that Mr. Arkan had entered the barracks and slapped the garrison commander. He had a rather unusual surname. And that he ordered that no troops could leave the barracks and come out of the compound.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, I want to draw your attention to your second visit to Bijeljina. Can you approximate for us your -- when that was.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-161
utterances.text: My second visit was a little later. Again, on the square there was a review of troops being carried out by a man known as Mauzer. There were about 500 soldiers lined up. There were also a large number of citizens seeing the soldiers off, who got into the bus and went off in the direction of Brcko.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: These people, these 500 that you're referring to, were they armed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-161
utterances.text: Yes. They were all armed, and they were also wearing military wartime uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Do you know what the purpose of these 500 was for going to Brcko?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-161
utterances.text: They said that they were going to defend Brcko.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, during this second visit, without telling us the identity or the relationship to you of the person involved, were you asked to carry a Muslim family out of Bijeljina?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-161
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Why were you asked to do that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-161
utterances.text: [redacted].

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: What was the family afraid of?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-161
utterances.text: They were afraid -- actually, there were individual incidents where people had been killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: What was the ethnicity of the people that you were asked to bring out of Bijeljina?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-161
utterances.text: They were Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And did they fear being killed because they were Muslim?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-161
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: How is it you were able to carry this family out of Bijeljina without being stopped?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-161
utterances.text: I had a vehicle with official licence plates, so I wasn't stopped.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And where did you bring them to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-161
utterances.text: I took them to Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I want to now draw your attention to Zvornik. Did you go to the municipality of Zvornik during this time period?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-161
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can you please describe for us when it was you first went to Zvornik during this time period.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-161
utterances.text: I went to Mali Zvornik first, and it was on the evening when the war broke out, a part of Zvornik, and the settlement was called Karakaj, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And can you describe your observations of Karakaj at that time.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-161
utterances.text: I noticed in Karakaj -- or, rather, I saw Mr. Marko Pejic once again, and he was in a textile factory over there. And up on the first floor there was a sort of production hall, and he had his headquarters there. And there were lots of soldiers coming and going up in front. They were going off somewhere else, I don't know where. And at the time that I arrived, I heard a piece of information according to which Fadil Mujic had been captured. And some people ran past me -- two soldiers, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt you, but could I ask you to move your chair a little bit closer to the desk. Apparently they're having difficulty picking up your voice on the microphone. And, sir, let me ask you a few more specific questions before you move on. Did you eventually learn how Peja came to be in Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-161
utterances.text: I was told that they were brought in by a gentleman from the local authorities in Zvornik and they were paid, being paid for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And who is the person who told you that they were being paid?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-161
utterances.text: People from the local leadership of the Zvornik municipality told me about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'd ask you to say their name or, if you're unable to, with the Court's permission I would ask you to refer to them by Prosecution Exhibit 450, tab 2. Can you tell us the number next to the name of the person who told you this information. Can you refer to the person who told you this information by the number on tab 2.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-161
utterances.text: Yes. He's under number 9 and number 12.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Could I ask you to tell us specifically what number 9, the person next to number 9, what he told you about the circumstances surrounding Arkan or Peja coming to Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-161
utterances.text: This individual told me that they had personally gone to Bijeljina and taken 400.000 German marks there, that that was the sum that the commander of the Tigers had asked for, and that he handed over the money. Later on, it was rumoured that he didn't give 400 but 250 and that he left 150 -- kept 150 for himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, I want to ask you about the conditions at the border between Serbia and Bosnia at this time. Were you able to see whether or not there were any checkpoints manned by members of the Serbian MUP?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-161
utterances.text: On the Serbian side there weren't any. The checkpoints hadn't been set up yet. However, there were some on the other side. On the Bosnian side there were checkpoints.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Who manned the checkpoints on the Bosnian side?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-161
utterances.text: They were manned by some soldiers. And there were people wearing police uniforms as well, as well as people from the various paramilitary units.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: You've identified three different groups. Would you clarify for us, are you saying that these three groups were intermingled in this function or they were manning separate checkpoints?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-161
utterances.text: Each of them were separate. Some held the depth, some were at the entrance, others in the rear. There were quite a few people who had been mobilised there too wearing uniforms of the old JNA army, the reservists.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did there come a time when checkpoints were established on the Serbian side of the border?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-161
utterances.text: Yes. A little later on, the checkpoints were set up there too on the side of Serbia. And the task was to prevent looting and passage with long rifles and uniforms that did not belong to the state of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did you ever have occasion to see paramilitaries on the Bosnian side of these checkpoints, at these border controls, preparing themselves to cross into the Serbian side?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-161
utterances.text: Yes. They would strip and put on sports gear; trainers, tracksuits. And I'm sure they did cross over at times. That's what was rumoured. They were said to take -- be taking the war booty back into Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: On the occasions that you saw them changing their clothes, did you see what they did with their weapons?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-161
utterances.text: I don't know where they left them. Probably with their units. But they had short-barrelled weapons. Sometimes what happened was that they would be searched, and then the people conducting the search would find weapons in the boots of their cars.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Are you aware of any occasion on which some of these people who weapons were discovered on in the boots of their cars were taken into custody?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-161
utterances.text: Yes, people were detained and their weapons confiscated.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Would that have been a routine occurrence?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-161
utterances.text: Yes, it would happen on a routine basis until permanent checkpoints were established where the police and the army would join together to prevent individuals crossing. If they would find somebody wearing police uniforms, then it would be the military police who would take them into custody. If not, then it would be the regular soldiers, the regular army who would do this.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, I want to draw your attention to this first time you were in Zvornik, and in particular to the small metal bridge in Zvornik of the several bridges or the two bridges there. Can I ask you to describe what you observed on that bridge during your first visit.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-161
utterances.text: Two bridges.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can I ask you to describe your observations about the smaller, the iron bridge on your first visit to Zvornik during this time period.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-161
utterances.text: I passed through Mali Zvornik, and getting off the bridge, a mass of citizens had gathered together, mostly women and children. They were in a panic. They were screaming. And I heard them saying, "They're killing over there." And they would turn to the left and went -- go into the settlement on the Serbian side.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I want to ask you -- I want to ask you to look at the list, tab 2 of 450, Prosecution Exhibit 450, and draw your attention to the person whose name is marked by the number 10. Did you make contact with this person after your arrival in Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-161
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can you describe for us what this person told you about what was happening in Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-161
utterances.text: I called up on the phone the main boss - and I don't see his name on the list here - and I talked to him. After several conversations, because we were agreeing about something, the other gentleman under number 10 came on the line and said that he didn't know where his boss had gone to, and he told me that Zvornik had been attacked and that Zvornik had almost been emptied of its citizens, and that he was alone, left alone in the building he worked in, and that he didn't know what was going on either. He said that there were four soldiers that had been taken into custody and were in detention. I asked who they were and he said, "Well, I don't know who they are either. They have several different documents on them, several different party membership cards." And I said, "Well, what parties?" And he said, "Well, they have ID cards belonging to the Radical Party." And then I told him once again that he should come over to me and that I would guarantee that nothing would happen to him. And he said to come over where, because the bridges were blocked. And I told him to go to the hydroelectric power plant.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, did you agree to remain in close contact with this person over the course of your time in Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-161
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: During this initial period when you went to Zvornik, how long did you stay there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-161
utterances.text: I stayed there two days and two nights.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did there come another time when you saw Peja during this trip to Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-161
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Where was that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-161
utterances.text: The first time was when I saw him at his headquarters, and the second time was several days later when he came to report that the town of Zvornik was a free town.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Are you familiar with the Alhos factory? That's A-l-h-o-s.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-161
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And for what purpose was that factory used during this time period?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-161
utterances.text: During that time period, it was where the command, the headquarters of all those units was, all the units that were stationed in Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did there come a time when you came to learn that number 10 on tab 2, that person, was arrested?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-161
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can you describe the circumstances under which you learnt that.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-161
utterances.text: When I went up the stairs of this Alhos headquarters building, I heard two soldiers running down the corridor, going past me, and saying that Fadil Mujic had been captured. And I remembered where he had been, so I went up to my car quickly, rushed after them. They drove fairly quickly, and they came to the door. I was right behind them, and I said, "Guys, this is Serbia, there is no war going on here. Go back to where you came from." They looked at each other and in fact returned. They didn't succeed in seeing Fadil. I entered. I was a little angry with Fadil, actually, and took him back to the hotel again where he waited for me, and the next day, I took him to the place from which he went abroad from.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did there come a time when there was a discussion about what was going on in Sepak?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-161
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And can you summarise for us, what was the concern or what was being said about what was occurring in Sepak?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-161
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Pavlovic told me that I should protect -- that I was protecting Fadil and that his Sepak was armed to a great extent and that it was only a question of time when they would attack the surrounding villages. Fadil said to me - and I believed him - that that was not true and that he had been there two days before and that he didn't believe in anything of that kind. I told Pavlovic this, and he suggested that if that was indeed so, we should all go there together with Fadil and convince ourselves that that was actually so. So we went in the evening, and that is why we postponed taking Fadil away. We postponed it by one day. We went there, but I myself didn't enter the village because Fadil told me not to. Marko Pavlovic went off, and so did Fadil and another friend of mine, and I myself and another gentleman stayed, that is to say number 9 on this document, stayed behind, did not enter the village. When I convinced Marko -- actually, they had reached an agreement that nobody would attack anybody and that they would hand over the weapons they had, and I just heard about what happened later on, several days later.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-161
utterances.text: And that is that those people had left all together to Loznica.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sepak, is that a village in the municipality of Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-161
utterances.text: Yes, it is a village in the municipality of Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can I draw your attention now to Marko Pavlovic, and ask you, when was the first time that you met Marko Pavlovic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-161
utterances.text: I met Marko Pavlovic for the first time the day after the war had started. And he introduced himself and said that he was a native of the area around Zvornik, the Sekovici municipality, and he showed me his ID card.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Were you able to see where that ID card was issued?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-161
utterances.text: The ID card was issued in the SUP of Sekovici.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And what was the name on the ID card?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-161
utterances.text: The name was Marko Pavlovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Was this an ordinary civilian identification card or was it belonging to any type of government organisation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-161
utterances.text: It was an ordinary ID card, the type that all citizens carry with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: After your first meeting with Marko Pavlovic, did he show you a document which described his official capacity in the municipality of Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-161
utterances.text: Yes. Sometime later, he showed me a document saying that he had been appointed chief of the Territorial Defence of Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I want to now draw your attention to Mr. Sekanic. You testified earlier that he was Marko Pavlovic's assistant or deputy. Could you tell us in a little more detail what his role and responsibilities were in Zvornik at that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-161
utterances.text: He was in command of a group of people who had been mobilised from the surrounding parts. And on one occasion, my brother was actually mobilised, so I went to see where he was, and I asked him who his commander was, and he said the commander was in the field. The commander came a little later and I said that my brother was not capable of doing military service, he wasn't military fit, and he said, "Well, take him home, then." And that's what I did. I took him home.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Are you able to say whether it was before or after the end of May 1992?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-161
utterances.text: It was sometime during that period. Perhaps the end of May or beginning of June.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did you become aware that both Sekanic and Marko Pavlovic were involved in the transportation of weapons?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-161
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can you please describe what you know about that.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-161
utterances.text: Sekanic told me that he was astounded at how Marko Pavlovic was able to enter the barracks at any time at all; during the night or whenever.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: When he used the word "barracks," what did you take that to mean? What type of barracks?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-161
utterances.text: They were military barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And what quantity of weapons was he describing to you they were able to get?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-161
utterances.text: Well, they were taken in trucks, truckloads.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Were there other people in Zvornik that were also involved in the transporting of weapons?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-161
utterances.text: Yes. The person under number 9.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And anyone else?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-161
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can you describe what you know about number 9's involvement in the transportation of weapons.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-161
utterances.text: He said that he had gone earlier, before the war began, and that he was with another person. Let me just see if his name is on this list.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I would ask you to only refer to them by number if it's essential to protect your identity.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-161
utterances.text: Yes. No, the person isn't on the list.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Are you able to say their name in open session?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-161
utterances.text: Yes. Well, you mentioned him at the beginning. It was Rade Kostic, but I can't see his name here.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And what was his involvement in this transportation of weapons?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-161
utterances.text: Well, person number 9 said he had gone to see him over there and that he gave him a truckload of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did there come a time when you spoke with somebody, a member of the SPS party, with respect to what you saw in Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-161
utterances.text: Yes, there did.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Who was it that you spoke to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-161
utterances.text: That person is number 2 on the list.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Why did you choose number 2 on this list to go and tell about what you had seen in Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-161
utterances.text: We were good friends.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did you ask him to convey your observations to anyone else?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-161
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can you please describe them.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-161
utterances.text: He said that in the evening, Mr. Nikola Sainovic would come to see him and that it would be a good idea if I came too, and that's what I did. I went there that evening and was in the house of number 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And did you inform Nikola Sainovic about your observations in Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-161
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I said that the civilians were under threat there quite a lot and that some illogical things were going on generally down there.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your -- what was your ultimate intention behind speaking to these two men about what you saw in Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-161
utterances.text: Well, I had expected them to convey this to the top leadership, nothing else, so that they should know what was going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can you be more specific about who you mean by the top leadership?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-161
utterances.text: I thought that the president would learn about it as well, Milosevic, because they had occasion to tell him that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can you give us your best recollection as to when you had this conversation with Nikola Sainovic.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-161
utterances.text: This was in April 1992, several days after the events in Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, would that be a convenient place to take the morning break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Witness B-161, could you remember to not speak to anybody about your evidence until it's over, and that does include the members of the Prosecution team. We will adjourn now for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, I'd like to now draw your attention to several days after the conflict broke out in Zvornik, and I want to draw your attention once again to the Alhos factory. Did you attend --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That's the textile factory, is it, that was referred to, Alhos?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did you go to that place once again?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-161
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can you describe for the Chamber how it was you came to go to that place and for what purpose.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-161
utterances.text: I was going there, in that direction anyway, to see where my relatives were, and someone from the local authorities told me that there was a meeting in Alhos and that I should go there if I could. So I went there. There were tables lined up in the conference hall up there. Downstairs, there were some soldiers moving around, roughly platoon strength, not more. I saw that the commander of one group was Zuco, the commander of another someone called Pusula, and a third by one of those mobilised people. I went upstairs. There were people sitting around the tables, and at one point a gentleman in uniform, the uniform of the army of Yugoslavia, walked in. In front of him, Major Pejic reported to him that the town of Zvornik had been liberated, and he said, "Major Marko Pejic reporting," and this gentleman responded, "No, I'm sorry, Lieutenant Colonel Marko Pejic." And he said, "I understand, Colonel." I may have commented ironically, saying, "Colonel?" He gave me a glance and said, "No, only one person here can be a colonel." He was asked to stay. There were some refreshments and some drinks, non-alcoholic drinks. He said that he didn't have time, that he had a lot of work to do in the field. He didn't sit down. He stayed for a couple of minutes, and then Mr. Pejic quickly went to pick up the phone --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, if I can just interrupt you there and ask you some detailed questions prior to this next area that you're about to talk about. The last few sentences of your testimony, you're referring to a person, you're saying "he," and "he had a lot of work to do." Who is the "he" that you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-161
utterances.text: He was Colonel Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, approximately how many people altogether were at this gathering or this meeting?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-161
utterances.text: There were, I'm sure, at least 30 people. There were the commanders of these various units, then there were some people from the local leadership, then there was Colonel Milosevic with some four members of his escort.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, I'm going to ask you to tell us the names of people that you recall being there. I'm going to ask you first to start with -- you say commanders of various units. Can I ask you to tell us the names of the commanders, if you know, or of the units that they commanded.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-161
utterances.text: Yes. There were several commanders that I didn't know, but I do know two of them. There was commander Vojin Vuckovic, then there was a commander whose wartime rank was colonel. They said he was somebody called Pusula, a local commander. And I didn't know any other commanders. I only knew the people who had been mobilised. I knew many people that I saw in front of Alhos.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, of the units that you didn't know the commanders, did you know the name of the units themselves?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-161
utterances.text: I don't know the names of those units, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, with respect to the other people present, were there any other people that -- present who were not paramilitary, not military, but other people from the municipality? If you know their names, I'd ask you to describe them for us.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-161
utterances.text: Yes, there were people in civilian clothes. Mr. Brano Grujic was there, Marko Pavlovic, Aco Sekanic, and some other people in civilian dress from the municipality that I don't know. This was very brief. Mr. Pejic said that in the evening, at 6:00, he would celebrate his promotion, and he invited all those present to come. I heard that in the evening they did celebrate. I wasn't there. I left.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, we must take this rather more rapidly, if we can, please. Witness B-161, it's very helpful to have your recollection of what occurred, but if you'd just concentrate on the questions which counsel asks, since we have a great deal of detail to get through.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Just a few more detailed questions about this. When Colonel Milosevic entered the room, did Pejic salute him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-161
utterances.text: Yes, he did. He saluted him and reported in line with military rules.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, Colonel Milosevic, did he return the salute?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-161
utterances.text: Yes, he returned the salute as envisaged by regulations.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And was it your understanding that by what Colonel Milosevic said to Pejic he promoted him on that occasion from a Major to a Lieutenant Colonel? Is that your understanding of what Colonel Milosevic did?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-161
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, were you present when Pejic made a phone call directly after this event?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-161
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Who did he call?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-161
utterances.text: He called Mr. Raznjatovic and said that Colonel Milosevic had promoted him to the rank of lieutenant colonel. The other one responded - there was a microphone attached to the telephone - "If the 'Komunjara' has promoted you to lieutenant colonel, I am now promoting you to the rank of colonel," and he said, "I understand," and he asked that the rank insignia be attached to his uniform. There were a couple of ladies present as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Was the phone on speaker phone? Were you able to hear Arkan speaking on the phone or did Peja tell you about what he said afterwards?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-161
utterances.text: Yes, everyone present could hear it because it was on the microphone. Speaker, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did there come a time when you became aware of members of Arkan's men committing crimes in the hospital in Mali Zvornik or in Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-161
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did you obtain Arkan's phone number and call him and personally inform him of what you had learned?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-161
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: What was his response?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-161
utterances.text: He shouted, and he said, "Shoot all those there." And I said, "It's your army, not mine. Come and shoot them yourself."

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And what happened?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-161
utterances.text: I met Arkan the next day, in the morning, on the road. They told me that he had been there, that he had lined up his troops, that he had sentenced two to death, and that he had driven them off with him. This was the story told by citizens.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, during the summer of 1992, did you have an opportunity to see a person known as Captain Dragan in Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-161
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: How many times?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-161
utterances.text: I saw him only once over there. There was an incident, and he was involved in that incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: The incident that you're talking about, was it during the takeover of the town or did it occur sometime after fighting had subsided in the town?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-161
utterances.text: It was sometime after the fighting in town had stopped.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can I ask you, in a sentence or two, to summarise the event that you witnessed having to do with Captain Dragan.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-161
utterances.text: One day, in the early evening, the local radio broadcast the news that terrorists had entered the town of Zvornik. The citizens were disturbed. We were sitting in Mali Zvornik, and we saw citizens looking in the direction of Zvornik, and we could hear bursts of fire across the Drina River. We went to the riverbank, and we saw soldiers going towards a settlement downstream on both sides of the river and searching the riverbanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did you see -- did there come a time when there was a man standing next at the edge of the riverbank, a Muslim man?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-161
utterances.text: Yes. I saw a man stepping into the river and hiding and going upstream slowly. Above him was a kind of embankment. People were shooting, and at one point the man was hit and he fell into the river. He was hit by the group of soldiers that were searching the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Were you able to tell whether that man was armed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-161
utterances.text: No. It was a man in civilian clothes. It wasn't far away, maybe 150 to 200 metres away from us. The citizens were saying that they saw another man that was wounded but who managed to swim across the river to Serbia. I got into a car and went across the river, across the pedestrian bridge, and there I came across the column of men searching the area. There were between 60 and 80 of them. They were in -- had war paint on their faces. In front of them was an open jeep with the driver and Captain Dragan sitting to his right. I stopped the car and said, "Mister --" or, "Captain, don't do any more nonsense. It would be best for you to leave as soon as possible." He just looked at me. I got into the car and left.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did there also come a time when you had a conversation with Aco Sekanic regarding an exercise that Captain Dragan was using -- in which he was using captured Muslim prisoners?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-161
utterances.text: Yes. He said, "That crazy captain has come and he took three captured Muslims and said that he would release them, but actually he's training his soldiers using them." After that, there was a meeting at which it was requested that he leave the municipality of Zvornik. He had a similar such meeting with General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, I'm going to now ask that you be shown Prosecution Exhibit 450, tab 7. And I want to first draw your attention to the last page of that document, and my question to you is: On the last page, do you recognise any of the names on that last page?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-161
utterances.text: Yes, I do know Mr. Mihajlovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And what is his first name?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-161
utterances.text: His first name is Petar.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And what were his responsibilities during this period of time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-161
utterances.text: He was head of the department for borders, border crossings and aliens in the Federal Secretariat for Internal Affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Was he involved in any activities with respect to the --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Mike, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Was he involved in any activities with respect to cooperation between different police departments?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-161
utterances.text: Yes. He said that he was coordinator for all the republics, that he also visited Slovenia, all the republics of the former Yugoslavia, therefore, and that he had been appointed to that duty by his federal minister, that is General Petar Gracanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I want to draw your attention to the first page of this document. And I would simply ask you to read the top endorsements on this document, first the endorsement on the left-hand side and then the one on the right-hand side.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-161
utterances.text: "The Federal Secretariat for Internal Affairs, third management, state security service, Belgrade, 23 March 1992, strictly confidential, Saradnja cooperation," number so-and-so. "Recent information and observations with regard to the security situation in the Bihac region."

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-161
utterances.text: Shall I read on?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: No. The Chamber will be able to read that later on. I want to now draw your attention to the Karakaj Technical School. Are you aware of that place and can you tell us where it is?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-161
utterances.text: Yes, I do know the place. I have quite a number of friends there. The locality is just close to Zvornik. The school is on the right-hand side from the direction of Bijeljina towards Zvornik. I later learnt --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, that's what I want to draw your attention to. Did there come a time after 1992 that you learnt about something that occurred in the confines of that school?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-161
utterances.text: Yes. I learnt that there were many people detained there and that they had all been killed and buried in a mass grave somewhere nearby.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Who told you this information?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-161
utterances.text: I heard this information from citizens, from friends from that locality. And later on, I was given more details by the president of the municipality, Mr. Brano Grujic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can you tell us approximately how many people Brano Grujic told you were killed in that school?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-161
utterances.text: He told me that more than 700 men had been detained there, 740. They weren't killed there. They were taken away from that place and killed somewhere else, and that it wasn't upon his orders but that one of his associates had given the order. Let me see now. He's under number 13.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And that's number 13 of tab 2. Did he tell you who actually committed the crimes?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-161
utterances.text: He told me that the crime had been committed by a group of Yellow Wasps. There was a group from Pivarski and Niski that I didn't know, and that these men had been prepared for an exchange for Serbs from Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did he indicate to you whether or not a person -- the person indicated under number 6 on tab 2, whether he had any involvement in the events at Karakaj?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-161
utterances.text: Yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Please describe what involvement this person had.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-161
utterances.text: That person coordinated all those paramilitary units, and he complained to us about those units, but we saw that he was closely connected to them. And when the time came to arrest one of the leaders of those paramilitary units under pressure of citizens who were saying that they were committing grave crimes against all ethnicities.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, I want to now draw your attention to a different area, and I want to begin by asking you, do you know a person by the name of Branko Ostojic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-161
utterances.text: Yes, I do. He's listed as number 18.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can I ask you, do you know this person personally?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-161
utterances.text: Yes, I know him well.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can you, in a sentence, describe what role or position he had during this time period.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-161
utterances.text: He was the vice-president of the government of Republika Srpska in charge of economic affairs. And he was a prominent member of the SDS party.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did he ever have a discussion with you with respect to bills that he paid for members of the RS leadership in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-161
utterances.text: Yes. He said that those bills had cost him $1.2 million.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did he tell you who he paid those bills for and the circumstances surrounding the payment of those bills?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-161
utterances.text: He said that he paid the bills for the entire leadership of Republika Srpska at the Intercontinental Hotel, that those were bills that they had incurred and that he was surprised that the drivers had made more telephone calls than the leaders.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can you tell us the names of the leaders who he indicated were -- these bills were for.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-161
utterances.text: According to what he said, there was Mr. Radovan Karadzic, Mr. Momcilo Krajisnik, the Prime Minister Lukic, some deputies, and their assistants, like drivers and bodyguards.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did he indicate to you what was the purpose of their stays in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-161
utterances.text: He didn't say what the purpose was, but it was to consult with the leadership of the state of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And did he indicate to you what period of time this occurred?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-161
utterances.text: This occurred before the beginning of the war and at the very beginning and for the next two years.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did he describe for you the relationship between Mr. Krajisnik and Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-161
utterances.text: Yes. He often spoke about that relationship. He said he didn't understand why Karadzic had so much trust in Krajisnik, because in his opinion, Krajisnik was a man who was not working well for his own people.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did he describe the relationship between Mr. Krajisnik and Mr. Jovica Stanisic of the Serbian MUP?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-161
utterances.text: No, he didn't go into any detailed explanations of that relationship.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did he describe anything with respect to the appointment of the criminal service bureau, the CSB, chiefs in the Podrinje area?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-161
utterances.text: I don't know which chief you're referring to, of what location.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Do you recall Mr. Ostojic saying anything with respect to these appointments?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-161
utterances.text: Yes. He was dissatisfied with the appointment of the head of the MUP of Republika Srpska and other chiefs of security centres, saying that they were mostly Krajisnik's men and that it wasn't in order that Mr. Karadzic had more trust in Mr. Krajisnik than in anyone else.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I want to now draw your attention to mid-July of 1995 and ask you, were you once again in the Zvornik area at that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-161
utterances.text: Yes, I was. I was in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Were you in a village in the area during which time you saw a group of people?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-161
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can you tell us how large the group of people were and where precisely they were, without -- not necessarily telling us the name of the exact village.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-161
utterances.text: There were up to 50 women and children there in front who were in front of a school playground. The playground was full of buses and soldiers of some kind who also had their faces painted in African colours. I stopped for a moment there and received some information, upon which I left and went to the command of the army of Republika Srpska in Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Before you left the village, did you ask the people or did they tell you what was going on in that area?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-161
utterances.text: They told me that they were killing people from Srebrenica there, and bursts of fire could be heard frequently.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Were you yourself able to hear the gunfire?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-161
utterances.text: Yes. I too heard the gunfire. It was about 100 metres from the road.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I interrupted you when you said -- you were beginning to say you went to report this to someone. Can you tell us precisely who it was you reported this observation to.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-161
utterances.text: I went there with a friend of mine, and I was looking for the head or the chief of that army by name, or anyone among the leaders. The man on duty told me that none of the leading people were there but that he expected somebody to come shortly. After awhile, a man did appear, a lower-ranked officer. He was cursing, and he said, "What are these Serbs like when they refuse to kill?" that he had to do it. And I said, "How could you do any such thing?" And he was surprised and -- as if he expected me to know that Mr. Beara had given such an order. I heard the name for the first time. I didn't know his first name. Then I retorted something rather roughly, and then I left.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can you tell us precisely what this person said about who ordered him to do what?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-161
utterances.text: He said that Beara had ordered that 6.900 people had to disappear within five days, from Zvornik southwards towards Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can you describe how that person looked, was there anything unusual about his physical appearance?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-161
utterances.text: Yes, He didn't have a cap on his head. He was wearing a soldier's shirt of some sort. He was all covered in soot, black from... He said: "I had to pick up a weapon myself and shoot." He looked somewhat disturbed, as though he was in haste. I asked what his name was. I was told the first name. I later learnt the surname as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: What was his name?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-161
utterances.text: His name was Drago. Later, I heard that he was Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: You said earlier, or the transcript records you as saying that the -- bodies had to travel from Zvornik to Bijeljina. Did the transcript record your answer correctly?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-161
utterances.text: For the bodies to go from Zvornik to Bijeljina? That doesn't sound right to me. Maybe in the direction of Bijeljina, not as far as Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can I ask you, just for the sake of clarity, can you please say again what it was that this person who you later learnt to be Nikolic, what exactly it was that he said to you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-161
utterances.text: Nikolic said that between Zvornik and southward towards Bijeljina, 6.900 men needed to be killed within five days. They were transporting live men to various villages and killing them. They did not enter the territory of Bijeljina municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to draw your attention --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Can I clarify this account. Who was it who told you, first of all, in the village or wherever it was that they were shooting people from Srebrenica? Who told you that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The locals told me, who were protesting and who disapproved. A woman was protesting, and then this soldier headed towards her with a rifle in his hand. They said that they had brought several busloads there and that they were killing them behind the school.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And then you went to the command. Is this right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And there you met this officer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And he was Nikolic; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And he told you that somebody called Beara had given this order?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, may we go into private session for a brief moment to ask one question related to this?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, I'm going to ask you now to draw your attention to the years 1994 and 1995. During this time period, did you also have occasion to travel frequently in the area of Western Serbia and Eastern Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-161
utterances.text: Yes, that's right, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: During your travels in those areas, did you become familiar with convoys that would cross the border?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-161
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can I ask you first to tell us approximately how many different times did you personally see convoys crossing the border, either from Serbia to Bosnia or Bosnia to Serbia -- I'm sorry, Serbia to Republika Srpska, or Srpska to Serbia.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-161
utterances.text: Well, I saw that at least 50 times.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can you characterise the convoy for the Chamber? For example, tell us approximately how many vehicles would be in a convoy on any typical observation, and what types of vehicles they would be.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-161
utterances.text: They were large trucks, and during one night about 80 trucks would cross the bridge, from 30 to 80. The crossings were made at several bridges, and when fuel was being transported, they had to have the canvas awnings across the trucks. There were different loads. There were logs being transported, people said that wheat was being carried too. So there were different truckloads of different goods.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can you describe the licence plates of these vehicles? Did they identify the particular country or republic that they came from?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-161
utterances.text: The licence plates were from the Republika Srpska, all the towns there, and also from the Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Based upon your observations of these convoys and your conversations with other people who saw these convoys, are you able to estimate for the Chamber with what frequency these convoys went across between the two countries?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-161
utterances.text: Sometimes every evening, sometimes every other evening or every two or three days, and I think it was a very profitable convoy. Certain leaders from the MUP on both sides would make a lot of money, and so would certain politicians, local ones.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Was there an area or a particular location in Serbia across from Zvornik that was used as a staging area for these convoys?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-161
utterances.text: They would come in loaded up, then they would wait there on -- in a parking lot in front of the Ravnaja factory, a quarry there, and that's where they used the raw materials for that limestone factory. And the place itself was referred to as "the quarry."

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And did you on -- did you ever see vehicles waiting there, waiting to cross the Drina?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-161
utterances.text: Yes. I saw that on several occasions. And when the news was bandied about that everybody was making a profit and earning things, there was a commission set up in Republika Srpska, and one member of the commission said that each driver had to pay a thousand marks in order to be given a turn in crossing. And this bypassed all the rules that had been established for the passage of those convoys. I asked -- I apologise, but let me just say I asked who the money was going to, and they said, "To the MUP over there." And I said, "Well how much did you take in tonight?" And he said, "263.000 German marks in just one night." So each driver, in addition to all the other papers, had to have a thousand German marks with him to be allowed to cross on any particular evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: On the occasions where you personally saw convoys cross the border, can you please describe what border controls, if any, were on the Serbian side of the border.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-161
utterances.text: On the Serbian side, a leader from the administration for border crossings would always turn up, the border crossings and aliens department. And from the Bosnian side, there would also be a commission from a team set up for the convoys and one staff member from their MUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Were there any particular people that you recognised being present at the border crossing during the time that you saw a convoy crossing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-161
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can you please tell us their names.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-161
utterances.text: I would see quite often there the chief, Mr. Puzovic, and his assistant, Mr. Boro Peric, and sometimes their inspectors.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm going to ask that the witness now be shown Prosecution Exhibit 450, tab -- I'm sorry. This is a photocopy of Prosecution Exhibit 336, Your Honours, pages 28 and 29 from the map.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, I'm going to ask that you take a look at this document and ask you, do you recognise the marks made on this map?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Could I ask the usher, please, to place it on the overhead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do recognise the border crossings. On the first one, I saw Mr. Jesuric in front of the convoy, preparing --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, can I ask you, was it you who made the markings on this map?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-161
utterances.text: Yes, it was me.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm going to ask that it be placed on the table to your left. The usher will help you with that. I'm going to ask that you take the pointer that's in front of you. What do your marks on this map indicate?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-161
utterances.text: This first one up here is the border crossing -- the first mark denotes -- this circle and the Red Cross denotes the border crossing between Serbia and Republika Srpska, and the place is Sremska Raca, the actual crossing. This second one is another border crossing between the Republic of Serbia and Republika Srpska, and the border crossing is called Pavlovica Cuprija at the Dadovica place, municipality Dadovica, in front of the village of Popovi. And then the third location is the border crossing at a place between Veliki and Mali Zvornik, on the bridge there. And throughout the war and -- it was assigned for -- as a footpath, and it still is. Otherwise, it was used for regular general traffic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, the three marks that you've made on this map, are they all locations where you personally saw convoys crossing between Serbia and Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-161
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would ask, for the last few questions I have for the witness, that we go into private session, and this is with respect to my earlier request before the witness entered the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, I hope that with my questions I'm not going to disclose the witness's identity. That is something I do not wish to do. I do not wish to be doing that, because the witness is a secret witness, if I can put it that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you think there's any --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't want us to keep going into closed session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No, of course. But if you think there is an area in which there is a danger of that happening, then we'll deal with that in private session. But if you can avoid it by not asking questions which are liable to do that, then we can stay in open session. And I should tell the witness, if there is some question which you think might have that effect, then of course you can ask to go into private session yourself. Yes. Let's make a start.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, let's start off then with Bijeljina. I'll have some questions later on which I think you'll wish to hear in private session due to the witness's identity, but let's start off with Bijeljina. And this will not establish his identity but to a certain extent -- actually, you were a resident of that region, the region you're talking about, or, rather, you're a Serb for Bosnia, let me put it that way.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-161
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You worked in Serbia, did you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-161
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So when we're talking about Bijeljina, who brought the Serb volunteer guards of Zeljko Raznjatovic, Arkan, to Bijeljina in the first place?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-161
utterances.text: Well, people said that this was done by the local leadership of the Bijeljina municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And is Mauzer one of those local leaders?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-161
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And the rest of the people from the local leadership; is that right?
